ai-at-work.title: Anthropic’s Opus 4.6 is a smut-machine
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic forbids its Claude models from generating sexually explicit content. But a series of tests conducted by TechCrunch found that it didn't take much to get past the restriction.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic's latest Claude model (Opus 4.6) can be tricked into generating explicit sexual content despite the company's stated safeguards against it. This matters because many organizations are quietly deploying Claude into their digital workplace tools for content creation, customer service, and knowledge work, and a jailbroken AI is a compliance and brand risk nobody needs. The irony is rich: we spent decades trying to keep employees off adult websites, and now the risk is that the websites come built into the tools we're giving them.

ai-at-work.title: Nvidia just showed that the harness, not the AI model, is now the real hero
ai-at-work.excerpt: Nvidia research shows that AI agents can perform well, and not go off the deep end, through fine-tuning, even if the AI model isn't that great at the task.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nvidia's research demonstrates that you don't need a brilliant AI model to get good results, just the right constraints and fine-tuning wrapped around it. For digital workplace leaders, this is genuinely important because it means your AI investments might work better if you focus less on chasing the latest massive model and more on building proper guardrails and workflows around whatever you've got. Honestly, this feels like the AI world finally discovering what enterprise software learned decades ago: a mediocre tool with solid process beats a brilliant tool with no structure every single time.

ai-at-work.title: Starcloud raises $250 million for orbital data centers as launch options dry up
ai-at-work.excerpt: There's about to be a big fight to secure access to space.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Starcloud just raised a quarter billion dollars to build data centers in orbit, betting that traditional launch capacity won't keep up with demand. For digital workplace folks, this matters because your infrastructure assumptions are about to get weird: latency profiles, redundancy options, and where your data physically sits are all up for grabs. Here's my take: we spent thirty years consolidating everything into three cloud regions, and now someone's literally taking the conversation off-planet. The irony would be hilarious if the migration costs weren't going to be absolutely brutal.

ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence hardware startup Starcloud Inc. today announced that it has raised $250 million in funding at a $2.3 billion valuation. Investment firm Manhattan West led the deal. It was join
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Starcloud just grabbed a quarter billion dollars to build AI data centers in orbit, because apparently we needed to make computing even more remote than working from home. For digital workplace teams, this matters because AI infrastructure in space could eventually mean lower latency for processing massive workloads and better disaster recovery options, though we're talking years away. Personally, I give it five years before someone suggests we move the entire helpdesk to a satellite and calls it "cloud native."

tools-tech.title: A low-tech solution from the past may be your best defense against AI deepfakes
tools-tech.excerpt: AI-enabled identity theft is getting too sophisticated to have predictable tells anymore, so experts recommend answering with a seemingly old-fashioned approach.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Security experts are recommending low-tech verification methods like phone calls or in-person checks as the best defense against AI-generated deepfakes that fool traditional detection software. This matters because digital workplace security teams can't rely on automated tools alone anymore, and they need to build verification protocols that actually work in the real world. It's darkly funny that after decades of trying to digitize everything, we're circling back to the telephone call as our most reliable security measure, but honestly, it beats explaining to your CFO why someone cleaned out the company accounts using a convincing video of her voice.

tools-tech.title: New ‘Slack Code’ turns AI coding into a team activity
tools-tech.excerpt: With the launch of “Slack Code” channels, Slack this week introduced a new way for developers and non-tech staff to work collaboratively with coding agents. While Slack already integrates with several
tools-tech.dwp_take: Slack just launched Code channels that let multiple team members collaborate with AI coding agents in a shared workspace instead of each developer working with them solo. This matters because it potentially breaks down the silos where technical work happens in isolation, which is the whole point of a digital workplace. Look, I've seen plenty of "collaboration features" that nobody actually uses, so Slack Code's success will depend entirely on whether developers actually want their coding watched and interrupted by non-technical stakeholders in real time.

tools-tech.title: OpenAI adds an AI safety layer to detect misuse without retaining enterprise data
tools-tech.excerpt: OpenAI is adding a new safety capability that allows enterprises to detect misuse of its AI systems across multiple interactions without retaining prompts or responses, enabling risk monitoring while
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI built a safety monitoring system that spots misuse patterns across multiple conversations without actually storing the conversations themselves. This matters because enterprises finally have a real path to use generative AI while keeping sensitive data off OpenAI's servers, which was a genuine blocker for many organizations. Honestly, it's the kind of practical problem-solving we needed instead of another press release about "responsible AI," though I'll believe the implementation details when I see them deployed in the wild.

digital-culture.title: What I learned when I gave up my daily to-do list and tried ‘task-batching’
digital-culture.excerpt: When it comes to productivity, there is no shortage of tips. I’ve tried many of them (some of which I’ve written about for this publication). But in the end, I’ve largely stuck to a similar practice:
digital-culture.dwp_take: A Fast Company writer ditched daily to-do lists in favor of task-batching, grouping similar work together instead of tackling everything in priority order. This matters because digital workplace professionals are drowning in context-switching, and batching is one of the few productivity approaches that actually holds up under real-world chaos. Here's the thing though: we've known task-batching works for decades. The fact that someone just discovered it proves most of us still aren't doing it, which tells you everything about how broken our default work habits really are.

digital-culture.title: ‘Bah, humbug!’ Could employee apathy mean curtains for the traditional holiday party?
digital-culture.excerpt: People say they prefer cash or time off, though some argue office gatherings are still beneficial
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are ditching traditional holiday parties because employees increasingly say they'd rather have cash bonuses or extra time off instead. This matters because it forces HR and leadership to reconsider whether mandatory seasonal gatherings actually build culture or just waste the budget on mediocre catering and awkward small talk. Look, I've been to enough limp office parties to know that nobody's loyalty is being cemented over warm eggnog, so if people want their money or their time back, maybe that's just honest feedback we should finally listen to.

industry-news.excerpt: Google’s new Android verification flow adds a 24-hour wait for apps from unverified developers as broader identity checks approach. The post Google Tightens Android Sideloading: Unverified Apps Now Fa
industry-news.dwp_take: Google is forcing a 24-hour waiting period for Android apps from unverified developers, tightening controls around sideloading as part of broader identity verification efforts. This matters because many enterprise teams rely on custom internal apps and developer tools that don't go through official app stores, and delays like this create real friction in daily workflows. After three decades watching companies fight platform vendors over control, I'll say this: Google's playing security theater while making legitimate work harder, which is pretty much the tech industry's favorite move.

industry-news.dwp_take: Waymo built its own 5nm AI chips to handle the massive sensor processing load in its self-driving cars as it scales up operations. This matters to digital workplace folks because it shows how companies solving hard problems stop waiting for off-the-shelf solutions and start building infrastructure that fits their actual needs, not some vendor's roadmap. The irony is Waymo figured out what most enterprises still haven't: sometimes you have to get your hands dirty and build the thing yourself instead of hoping your current tech stack magically evolves.

industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft removed WMIC from a Windows 11 Beta build. Learn what the change means for security, legacy scripts, and supported replacement tools. The post Microsoft Removes WMIC From Windows 11 Beta: Wh
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft has removed WMIC (Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line) from Windows 11 Beta, forcing organizations to migrate away from a tool that's been around since Windows 95. This matters because plenty of IT departments still rely on WMIC scripts for system administration and automation, meaning your automation playbook just got a shelf life expiration date. The real kicker is that Microsoft had already deprecated this thing years ago, so if your organization hasn't planned the migration yet, you're essentially playing catch-up on a game that was already called.
